## 3. What's wrong with movies today. IMO

**Score:** 530
**Body:** I often find myself not being able to enjoy many of today's movies and I couldn't quite figure out why. My friends think it is crazy I am not into newer movies. Not all, but I find it difficult to enjoy most new movies.   
Then while watching Jaws Saturday, I think I know why. Most movies made today are too sterile. Meaning that they are filmed on a green screen in a controlled studio. There is no natural wind. There is no natural light. The sound is too isolated. None of it feels real. In Jaws, you can see and almost the wind gusts as it moves flags, jostles the hair on actors, and moves clothing. Naturally I may add.    
Now, add in all of the forced brand placement. If Toyota funds a project, every vehicle in that movie is a Toyota. That never happens in the real world. Everyone at a bar, beach party or festival are all drinking the same beer. Possible? Sure. Likely? No.   
Again, while watching Jaws, I can't think of a single brand I saw. This scene here is a perfect example. By today's standards, you'd see a dozen Coppertone bottles, cans and bottles of Cokes, Yeti coolers, Nike shirts, etc. 

Additionally, using big name actors today in movies and shows that are set in the wild west days are strange to me. I know the movie doesn't exist, but it's like putting Robert Pattinson or Brad Pitt into a role that was set in the pioneer days or earlier. Knowing they are big stars today just takes away the authenticity of the film. I think that's a reason that movies like Obsession do so well. There isn't a big Hollywood name in it. It's cast with people that feel like our friends and coworkers.   
  
Thoughts? For context, I am in my early 40's and should be obsessed with MCU, yet I've seen 1 and couldn't finish it. 

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I also feel like dialogue has taken a back seat to pretty visuals and special effects.
  - Not just dialogue, the *writing* in general takes a back seat to pretty visuals and big action sequences 
    - My theory is we used to get movies from people that read books, or maybe fought in a war. Today we get movies from people that grew up really into movies and now they write movies chock full of the things they saw in movies growing up. And most typically this manifests itself as garbage.
  - It’s not only the dialog, but the way dialog is spoken and recorded. I can’t hear WTF people are saying half the time because they no longer enunciate their words. They talk soft, low, and mumbly like they’re sitting across from the table at a quiet restaurant. It’s infuriating. It’s also the audio mixes that can’t seem to get the dialog volume right versus the environment. It makes me wonder what the hell their target device is.. or if they’re saying “fuck it, we do it fast and cheap.. people can turn on subtitles since the kids these days do it anyway”. Needless to say, I HATE subtitles. I want to watch my movies and shows, not read them.
2. Terrible pacing. Movies now days want to do a big unveil one after another after another when what made JAWS special was the build
  - A few months ago I watched *Zulu*.

Beyond the novelty of seeing a young Michael Caine without a cockney accent, one of the things that really stood out to me was just how patient the movie was.

The first 10 minutes or so are basically just watching a mass Zulu wedding ceremony. That's it. It lets the scene play out, lets you take in the people and the setting, and doesn't seem remotely worried that you might get bored because the plot hasn't started yet.

And the whole movie is like that. It takes its time when it needs to.

A modern movie could absolutely include the same opening sequence, but I'm pretty sure they'd compress it into about 15 seconds before cutting away to something more "important."

We've gotten very uncomfortable with just letting a scene breathe.
  - This sentiment clashes sharply with the new generations, who are perpetually distracted by screens; they are said to have 30-second attention spans. People no longer have the patience to wait and are unwilling to put in the effort to discover things—finding it boring or exhausting—which is certainly one of the reasons why.
3. So many cuts. Love a long take
4. Newer movies use very shallow depth of field and tight shots in order to reduce the work required to setup a background for the shot. I think that is what annoys me more from modern movies. What was a trait exclusive of direct-to-tv movies now is common in big budget productions. 

The image from Jaws you posted is a very good example of that, you can see they were trying the make the shot feel alive. 
5. I don't discredit your comment; I just think movie oversaturation plays a part. Some stuff just feels like churn and burn, dumped onto a platform or into a small theater run, creating a larger batch of movies. Movies weren't as easy to make years ago, so the pool wouldn't be diluted. 

With that said, you are also using Jaws as a comparison, which would be on a fair number of top ten lists of the greatest movies ever made

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Godard/Paul is dead?

**Score:** 34
**Body:** I watched the 1967 Jean-Luc Godard film Weekend recently. It’s a surreal masterpiece, much of it centering around a couple’s attempt to flee Paris because modern life has become impossible. But many other Parisians have gotten the same idea and there’s an absurd traffic jam on a small country road. Lots of wrecks ensue.  
At one point the driver learns that someone they know has died in a wreck, and he turns to his female companion and says ‘Paul is dead.’  
I thought Godard was riffing on the rumor. Then I realized that the Paul story started getting circulated after the movie.  
It’s the kind of celebrated avant-garde movie the Beatles would have certainly seen, and I idly wondered if they or someone else got the idea for the hoax/conspiracy from Godard.  
The death in a car accident evokes ADITL, of course, but time wise that has to be an artistic coincidence.  
Idle thoughts from a guy sitting in a hospital bed. Thanks for indulging me.

### Top 4 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. 

[IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0062480/locations/) says that *Weekend* was filmed:

> Sep 5, 1967 - Oct 12, 1967

While the "Paul is Dead" rumours [started a year earlier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_is_dead) in September 1966:

> Although rumours that Paul McCartney's health was deteriorating had existed since early 1966, reports that McCartney had died only started circulating in September of that year....

> In early 1967, the rumour resurfaced in London, this time claiming that Paul McCartney had been killed in a traffic accident while driving along the M1 motorway on 7 January. The rumour was acknowledged and rebutted in the February issue of The Beatles Book.  McCartney then alluded to the rumour during a press conference held about the release of Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band in May.
2. >It’s the kind of celebrated avant-garde movie the Beatles would have certainly seen, and I idly wondered if they or someone else got the idea for the hoax/conspiracy from Godard.

Like RunDNA said, the rumor started before Weekend was released. Well before my time, but I strongly suppose that if Godard had been the first one to say "Paul is dead" then it would've never taken off as a meme. "Paul is dead" I think was really kind of an organic, "from the people" kind of thing. A folk meme as it were if you ask me. 
3. Paul is meant to be Jean Pierre Leaud's character in Masculine Feminine (1966). He is literally dead at the end of Masc-Fem but the in-joke for Godard is that the persona of Jean Pierre Leaud's characters from 400 Blows onward has always been 'Paul'. Godard is declaring that the old world Paul is dead in the post-modern nightmare of France in Weekend.
4. I’ll venture a little theory here: there is a French expression used to refer to an unspecified individual or group of individuals—"Pierre, Paul, Jacques"—using the three first names that were most common in France for a long time; so, saying "Pierre, Paul, Jacques" is a way of speaking about an anonymous person.

 So, when Godard says "Paul is dead," he is essentially saying that "someone",an individualhas died. He is likely talking about the inevitability of death and the absurdity of life.

Then again, Godard was a bit of a prankster; he might also have been referring to someone he disagreed with... Jean-Paul Belmondo? Or Paul McCartney, with whom he had a conflict over a joint project that never materialized (though that was in 1968, so after "Weekend").

## 2. Has the cinema of Desplechin—the contemporary "Truffaut"—crossed France's borders ?

**Score:** 12
**Body:** I think I already have the answer, so apologies in advance for using Truffaut’s name to draw you to this post. However, it is only a half-truth, since Desplechin is arguably the French director who can most clearly be defined as the worthy successor to the great Truffaut.

They are common themes, a fondness for romance, and male characters who are melancholic and grappling with metaphysical questions. Both filmmakers also love ensemble film where characters reunite, part ways, and meet again etc.

Desplechin also shares a cinematic alter ego with Truffaut: the character Paul Dédalus, played by Mathieu Amalric (mirroring Truffaut’s Antoine Doinel—a character we watched grow up and age across four feature films and one medium-length film, the most famous being the first: The 400 Blows).

His cinema also remains true to the spirit of the New Wave: constant shifts in tone and explorations of different genres within a single film (with Desplechin, a movie might move from romantic comedy to spy thriller to adolescent coming-of-age story). There is also a highly theatrical, Brechtian approach; the memory of a conversation might transform into a stage play with theatrical sets for the duration of a scene.

He explores worlds such as high-ranking diplomacy, espionage, and forensic medicine, as well as the legal proceedings the protagonists face, all in an extremely naturalistic manner. Desplechin’s work also invariably features psychoanalytic sessions, secret letters, family dramas, and characters with sophisticated cultural references in literature and music. ( Most of Desplechin’s characters come from fairly bourgeois cultural backgrounds. )

And he has a rather unique tone, able to create strange and almost fantastical atmospheres when needed, but it all remains very grounded; let's talk about the mystery of existence that we all face.

Finally, Desplechin has also made three forays into the English-speaking world : Jimmy P. with Benicio del Toro (a psychoanalytic Western), Esther Khan (set in the 19th-century English theater world), and an adaptation of a Philip Roth novel ( adapted within a French context).

As for me, this best movie it's " Kings and Queen" tells a dual story: that of Ismaël, a suicidal musician forcibly committed to a psychiatric hospital, a confinement that looks very much like a conspiracy against him—and that of Nora, his ex-partner, who must deal with the imminent death of her writer father (and a mysterious diary associated with him). For those who enjoy TV series, it is something of a French "Six Feet Under". You will experience a whole range of emotions. And there is an incredible break-dancing moment...

The second film is \*A Christmas Tale\*, centering on a family gathering at Christmas around a matriarch who needs a bone marrow transplant. A real settling of scores takes place within the family. Nothing murderous—though, then again, maybe it is.

I’d be curious to know which of his films you have or haven’t seen from him ?

  
(Edit: English is not my native language; I apologize for any errors in syntax or grammar.)

### Top 0 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)


## 3. How do people feel about first person voice over narration in movies?

**Score:** 10
**Body:** I don’t see a lot of movies today using this narrative device. It seems like it was really common in the 90s. It works for a lot of movies that are based on first person narration books like fight club, American psycho, and fear and loathing in Las Vegas. But you also see it used in movies like forest gump and goodfellas. 

I loved these movies when I was in high school but at the same time it’s like people criticize clunky exposition and they resoundingly demand “show not tell”. But there seem to be ways to make it really engaging, play against the visual, add insight into inner thoughts that otherwise would have been impossible, and add that beat prose flair. 

Are these movies still getting made and I just haven’t seen them bc they’re just not good or popular? Or was it a 90s style that’s pretty much an anathema to sophisticated filmmaking that just gets avoided bc it feels like saying “that was Jimmy and he ate grass for a living before the plague hit” or “and that was that, my ambition dissolved with that single word ‘Parmesan’, I slumped into my proverbial chair into a pit of self loathing but I nonetheless obsequiously in a sycophantic tone ‘good for you!’” 

Do people hate stuff like that?

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Robert McGee is a script doctor who in the 80s started a screenwriting seminar. It became very popular within the industry and even had several Oscar winning screenwriters take his class. He also released a book summarizing the seminar in 1997. One of the core principles is about how first person narration is a lazy plot device. It spoonfeeds information to the audience when it's more rewarding and artistically pleasing to show not tell. So from the late 90s onward first person narration was phased out by writers who were influenced by McGee's seminar. 

The 2002 film Adaptation, Nicholas Cage plays a struggling writer who takes McGee's class, in the film played by Brian Cox. There's even a scene where Cage is talking to himself in his mind when McGee says that internal monologues should be avoided and Nicholas Cage immediately stops. 

McGee has later clarified that first person narration isn't automatically bad, but it does have its own time and place. Too many bad movies rely too much on it. Think of The Great Gatsby, where the narration is actually a therapy session. Or KickAss where the narration is mocking comic book structure. Or Society of Snow where narration is used to misdirect the audience as to who lives and died. You can still use first person narration, it's not automatically good or bad, just don't use it as a short cut
  - First-person narration can also be part of a genre's aesthetic identity, like film noir and neo-noir.
  - Oh shit, I forgot that part of adaptation. Yeah I figured there was actually like some pedagogue or critic made an argument about how it babies the audience or whatever. And yet, Hollywood makes movies with recycled IP and the worst of the worst contrived unnatural exposition high concept fantasy/sci-fi plots. 

Sure, I don’t care to be spoon-fed, but it’s a vibe especially if the narrator is unreliable which is like \*the\* thing you learn in high school as a thing to discuss in literature. 
2. Some of my favorite movies of all time use voiceover narration:

Days of Heaven  
Goodfellas  
The Royal Tenenbaums  
Taxi Driver  
Trainspotting  
Apocalypse Now

It’s a tool for a filmmaker to use like any other, and it’s often used poorly. But when it works and contributes to the film, it can be the one of the best parts of the film, as in Days of Heaven. 
  - In Apocalypse Now, it is used very sparingly—specifically when the character reads the military documents he has been given. Here, we have a perfect use of voice-over.
3. It gives the film a novelistic feel. Which makes perfect sense in Scorsese’s chronicles (or sometimes serves as a source of comic relief). Ultimately, it depends on what the film is trying to convey. 

In Godard’s films, it serves to break the traditional narrative, not merely as a gimmick, but as a form of commentary on the film itself. With Godard, there is also the idea of ​​producing a filmic document ; a testimony or a poetic philosophical statement.

At times, however, it is a resounding failure  in James Gray’s "Ad Astra" and, before that, Ridley Scott’s " Blade Runner". The visual storytelling is disrupted by a voiceover that induces sleep rather than providing insight. Incidentally,

 I would love to see Gray eventually release a version of "Ad Astra" without the voiceover. He's a filmmaker who has always adhered to the "clear line" style and theoretical schematism, and the voice-over really sabotaged this otherwise very beautiful film.
4. I think too often it gets used as a crutch. And honestly, I would bet a decent amount of narration of that kind is used to fill gaps from rewrites or areas where coverage was poor or the shots on the day just didn't work for some reason or another. Which is understandable, but there are ways to weave it into the storytelling without it feeling like it is just filling the role.

It's at its worst when it is used to talk down at an audience, like they didn't understand something. Maybe like in suicide squad, where a character runs through the lineup and says what everyone's powers are, instead of letting it feel lived in like say The Incredibles does it.

It's at its best in something like True Detective, where it is used to add a layer of complexity to a weaving mystery. Centering the narrative during non-linear storytelling by giving more impression to the audience how the narrating characters viewed the events of the past.
5. When I was in film school in the 70s, I was taught the same thing that a lot of you were taught, that it was lazy and usually unnecessary. I understand the attitude and the feeling, but I no longer agree with it as completely as I did before. I can’t imagine Goodfellas without the narration. I can’t imagine To Kill a Mockingbird without the narration. Obviously any films that Wes Anderson has done definitely need the narration lol. You just have to ask yourself if the narration adds or distracts from a movie. Barry Lyndon’s narration, for example, is a bit of a distraction. The narration in the Barbie film was cute but unnecessary. You just have to be very careful in using it. And let’s face it, if you’re doing a literary adaptation, the author has some beautiful words that you do not want to miss out on. Most Dickens adaptations do not use narration, but some really cry out for it. There would be no reason a version of Great Expectations couldn’t use the narration, especially in the final scene, which has never been adapted properly anyway.

For women, long black hair stood for beauty, health, and the soul. If you watch geisha movies, you'll notice they spend forever keeping their hair immaculate. When a character loses her mind, her hair instantly comes undone or falls out.

Since hair was basically tied to a person's soul, it naturally became a weapon for vengeance when a female spirit returned to haunt the living.

## 5. Léon the Professional - peaking into Léon’s perspective

**Score:** 7
**Body:** I’ve been binge watch react youtube videos about Léon lately and it made me realize what’s really happening.

I don’t want to go into the controversy too much, and not talk at all about the director, but I’ll say for those who haven’t seen the movie that Mathilda, a 12 year old, develops a crush on an old hitman. The rest will be filled with spoilers, so make sure to watch the movie if you haven’t recently. I’m going quite in depth and I’m basing my arguments on details that wouldn’t look crucial at a glance, so you might not remember them.

The movie insists a lot on Mathilda’s feelings, and we don’t have many clues about how Léon is living their relationship. Yet it’s the cornerstone of the controversy, and we’re left with hoping that Léon remains a father figure, or we’re disgusted that he doesn’t reject strongly this inapropriate dynamic.

There’s a quick scene in the extended cut where Leon tells his backstory, and it sheds a different light on his feelings if you take the time to go back and watch it again from the start.

Léon says that, when he was 19, he had a girlfriend who had to defy her family to be with him, but her father ended up killing her. I think this is something Léon has been stuck on ever since. He’s watering his plant like we would bring flowers on a grave. He is a sad man, still grieving for his teenage love and how life could have turned out different.

The first night he shelters Mathilda, Léon unambiguously treats her like the little girl she is. And in the middle of the night, he wakes up in quasi-panic, pulls a guy, goes to the room she sleeps, and points it at her head before getting a grasp on himself again and leaving.

With the backstory that we know, this is Léon re-living the tragedy of his youth, but from the perspective of the father who killed his girlfriend. Léon grew lonely, coarse, guilty, and deseperate. When Mathilda’s arrival forces him to opening up, his impulse leads him to killing, like the only experience he had ever known, until the realisation strikes him that he cannot become what he despised.

The movies goes on, and Léon oscillates between rejecting Mathilda’s presence and being a father figure for her. Unfortunately, Mathilda has her own arc, she’s at the beginning of her teenage years, she fancy’s herself a grown up, even a femme fatale, and every time Léon patronizes her or tries to grounds her into reality, she acts out, defiently romanticizes their relationship, and try to imposes to him that she is a woman.

It goes to the point where she confesses her love to him, which Léon reacts to with a lot of care and respect, aluding to the fact that Mathilda isn’t in love, but only feels safe for the first time in a life. Directly after this exchange, Léon goes to a job, and as he leaves the appartment, he leans onto the wall, apparently lost and emotionally stunned, deeply touched by how unprepared he must feel in front of this young girl growing. Maybe he is feeling like witnessing the behind-the-scene of his teenage year’s girlfriend, before she got killed and he feels crushed by the nostalgia.

When Léon gets back from this job we’re never shown, he’s wounded by a bullet he took at the height of the heart. There’s probably a hint in the editing, from the moment where Léon crumbles on the wall like he was hit by something and his coming back bleeding. Mathilda reopened a wound, and not only that, but, unhappy of her love not being recognized as such by Léon, she went in the hotel lobby and told the clercks that Léon and her were lovers.

After that, their relationship changes drastically. Léon stops trying to be a paternal figure, something Mathilda kept rejecting. He is not her father, and he won’t act as such anymore. This is the moment where the ambiguousness starts.

From the viewers perspective, we don’t know yet his backstory and his motive, and Léon never tells us anything. We’ve got to rely on the editing and the decisions he makes to understand his mindset until the scene where he explains his youth. He continues to train Mathilda as if nothing happened, he doesn’t even scold her for telling the clerck that they were lovers, and discreetly he starts to prepare his own plan.

A few scenes between them shows how much Léon is fed up by Mathilda’s behaviour. Though he keeps trying to protect her, two discussions turn into quasi-arguments, with him telling that he’s gone enough of her mindgames, to which Mathilda reacts dramatically, imposing that for her it would always be love or death, and imposing a russian roulette on herself, that Léon deflects at the last second.

Maybe that scene is a parallel to the events that got Léon young girlfriend killed. At the time, her family was considered "respectable" Léon says, and the police noted it as an accident.

Nevertheless, Léon, who always appears calm in front of Mathilda, starts to act out in his own way. He brings Mathilda to meet Tony, then comes back later to tell Tony that she’d be his heir. And he starts hunting down the police who killed Mathilda’s family. Clearly he knows that he’s going to be killed in avenging her.

Mathilda, emboldened by the new way Léon treats her, goes after Stanfield (Gary Oldman) on her own. Apparently, she thinks that if she makes her first hit by herself, she’d be woman enough to become her lover. A first time for a first time. Léon saves her life in the DEA office, and the same night he tells her his backstory. For the first time, we see Mathilda stops trying to force a romance on him.

Léon finally opened himself up, and with that he finalizes the sentimental education he was trying to give Mathilda. During the whole movie, he tried very hard to show her that she needed to take her time to grow up, to stop being brazen all the time, but to respect herself, keep distance with people and only open herself when she feels comfortable enough.

Now that Léon finally shares some of his own feelings with her, their relationship seems to reach a sort of harmony, but after the assault on the DEA office, Stanfield has found their trace and brings a SWAT team to take them out. Léon manages to find an escape for Mathilda, but she notices Léon wouldn’t be able to follow. He has to convince her to leave him, and the first words he pronounces are « Mathilda, we said no discussion », something he once told her about drinking her glass of milk. Unsues a touching attempts from Léon to get her to escape.

She descends down the vents, while Léon tries his escape disguised in a SWAT uniform. He reaches the final corridor, the light shines at the end in a way to reminisce Mathilda being saved the day her family was murdered, but Stansfield waiting on him, they both end up dying in an explosion. Léon sacrifices himself, and Mathilda gets to live.

Maybe Léon’s plan that would certainly lead him to death isn’t about Mathilda. If it was out of fatherly love, he wouldn’t have done something that would separate them. Léon’s action must be determined by the love his lost at 19, and that Mathilda brought back to his attention. Léon wanted to die, because he wanted to rejoin his soulmate. All the romance Mathilda forced on him rekindled the kind of love one nurtures for a deceased spouse. He also must have understood better what the father of his girlfriend would have gone through, and that’s why he chose to die taking Stanfield’s crew out. He washed his guilt, and finally pure and remorseless, he joins his love in death.

That’s my reading after numerous re-watchs and also looking a react videos on youtube, who brought to my attention many insights. Do you guys agree? Could Léon and Mathilda destinies cross each other, in this mutually beneficial exchange?
